chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Ibn Sinan said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who travels in the month of Ramadan and has a female servant with him, and he is permitted to have intercourse with her during the day. He said, 'Glory be to Allah, does this man not know the sanctity of the month of Ramadan? Indeed, he has a long night (to make up for it).' I said, 'Is it not permissible for him to eat, drink, and shorten (the prayer)?' He said, 'Indeed, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, granted the traveler permission to break the fast and shorten (the prayer) as a mercy and alleviation for the place of fatigue, exhaustion, and hardship of travel, and He did not grant him permission for intercourse with women while traveling during the day in the month of Ramadan. He obligated him to make up the fast, and did not obligate him to complete the prayer when he returns from his travel.' Then he said, 'And the Sunnah is not to be measured (by the minimum ruling), and indeed, when I travel in the month of Ramadan, I do not eat except the basic sustenance (qut) and I do not drink except until I am fully satisfied (riyy).'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a traveler having sexual intercourse during the day in Ramadan?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between the general concessions for travelers—breaking the fast and shortening prayers—and the specific prohibition of sexual intercourse during daylight hours in Ramadan, which invalidates the fast and requires only Qada (making up the days) rather than Kaffarah. He further highlights the superior Sunnah of minimal consumption (eating only 'al-quoot' and drinking only to quench thirst) to preserve the spiritual essence of fasting even while exempted. This narration underscores the Shia jurisprudential view that travel is a mercy for ease, not a license for full indulgence in Ramadan's sanctities.
